content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"The blind consensus is split between two main streams with several recognized alternatives: (1) the vulnerable outsider to whom hospitality is owed and in whom Christ is encountered (Matt 25, Lev 19, Heb 13:2); (2) believers as strangers/pilgrims on earth whose citizenship is in heaven (Heb 11:13, 1 Pet 2:11, Phil 3:20); (3) those alienated from God's covenant who are brought near in Christ (Eph 2:12,19); plus minority readings (false shepherd of John 10:5, Christ the unrecognized stranger). Two of four responses say no single settled consensus exists.","book_summary":"The book defines the stranger through a citizenship/covenant framework: a non-citizen of God's commonwealth — one outside the covenants of promise who is drawn in (Eph 2:12,19), and who, once inside, becomes in turn a stranger to the world. It cites only Ephesians 2:12,19 and cross-references Orphans, Widows & the Fatherless for the social-care dimension.","consensus_core_identification":"'Stranger' is a multi-stream symbol whose leading identifications are the vulnerable outsider to be welcomed (hospitality/Christ-in-the-stranger) and the believer as pilgrim-exile, with covenant alienation (Eph 2) as a well-attested further stream.","book_core_identification":"The stranger is defined by covenant citizenship status: one alienated from God's commonwealth who may be incorporated, whereupon the direction of estrangement reverses and the believer becomes a stranger to the world.","core_relation":"BOOK_NARROWS","extension_relation":"BOOK_SUBSET","boundary_disagreement":"The book elevates the Ephesians 2 covenant-alienation reading (Response C's primary; an alternative in A, B, D) to the sole defining sense and fuses it with the pilgrim reading (primary in B and D) as its second movement ('once in, made a stranger to the world'). It excludes from the definition the hospitality/vulnerable-outsider stream that Response A treats as primary and B calls dominant (Matt 25:35, Lev 19:33-34, Heb 13:2), relegating social-care material to a cross-reference, and it omits the negative uses (John 10:5 stranger-voice, the strange woman) and the Christ-as-Stranger devotional reading.","material_contradiction":"","rationale":"The book's identification is squarely within the consensus's recognized streams: covenant alienation (explicit in all four responses via Eph 2:12,19) and the believer-as-stranger-to-the-world (the pilgrim motif, primary in two responses). It does not replace the consensus referent; rather it selects and unifies two consensus streams into a single citizenship-reversal schema while cutting away the hospitality/ethical stream that much of the consensus treats as primary or dominant. That is a material boundary change — the ethical Matt 25/Lev 19 cases are reclassified out of the symbol's definition — but the central category (the outsider relative to God's people, capable of incorporation) remains intact. Hence REFINED with a narrowed extension, not DIVERGENT and not NOVEL.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue MATCH: since the consensus itself is split and Response C's primary meaning ('outsider to God's covenant people, capable of being welcomed and incorporated,' grounded in Eph 2:12,19) is nearly identical to the book's definition, the book merely picks one already-recognized primary. Against this, the book's exclusion of the hospitality stream from the definition and its distinctive two-directional reversal ('once in, made a stranger to the world') constitute a real boundary reshaping, and the cited verses do not support the stranger-to-the-world clause, so REFINED with PARTIAL citation support is the better fit.","confidence":"medium"}
